meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One man with a gun can control 100 without one'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lenin. The line is absent from his Collected Works; Wikiquote files it under Misattributed and dates its online appearance to the mid-1990s.

answer.label: Not Vladimir Lenin — an unsourced internet attribution
answer.authorDates: Origin unknown · surfaced online in the mid-1990s (per Wikiquote)
answer.sourceLine: No speech, article, letter or book by Lenin contains this line. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed: “Not found in Lenin’s Collected Works. Began to surface on the internet in the mid-1990s.” Who first wrote it is unknown.

source.heading: Where the line can be found, and where it can’t

docMeta.dd: No primary source: not found in any work by Lenin

source.excerpt: One man with a gun can control 100 without one.
trail: Wikiquote’s Lenin page ↗ lists the line under Misattributed, with the note “Not found in Lenin’s Collected Works. Began to surface on the internet in the mid-1990s.”
On the Wikiquote talk page ↗, the line has a discussion thread of its own: “I’ve seen this quote pop up a lot, but have never seen a credible source to back it up. Did Lenin really say this?”
Lenin’s real use of the phrase is in “From a Publicist’s Diary” ↗ (notes written 24–27 December 1917, first published 1929): theme one is “The man with the gun need no longer be feared.”
In a Straight Dope forum thread ↗, the line was posted with no source as one of a set of Lenin quotes about guns. Another participant pointed out that none of them appear on Lenin’s Wikiquote page.
source.excerptNote: Since no source text by Lenin has been found, there is no fuller passage to quote. The wording above is how the line circulates, often in lists of gun-related quotes credited to Lenin. A variant reads “a hundred” in place of “100”.
source.rightsNote: The wording cannot be traced to any work by Lenin or to any other identifiable author or first publication, so Quotle.info makes no claim about its copyright status. Lenin’s own “man with the gun” note is a different text.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: What Lenin actually wrote about “the man with the gun”
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary, Bolshevik leader and founder of Soviet Russia
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin led the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917 and headed the Soviet government until his death in 1924. His writings and speeches fill dozens of volumes of Collected Works, and this line is not in them. He did use the phrase “the man with the gun”. In a set of notes he wrote in Finland in late December 1917, he listed as a theme to write up: “The man with the gun need no longer be feared.” That is close to the opposite of the meme.

misattribution.heading: How a modern line got a revolutionary’s name
misattribution.intro: The sentence circulates as Lenin’s, often next to other gun-policy “Lenin quotes”. None of them comes with a speech, an article or a date.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Misattributed section and says it is not found in Lenin’s Collected Works. It also says the line began to surface online in the mid-1990s, about seventy years after Lenin died.
In a Straight Dope forum thread ↗, the line appears with no citation in a set of Lenin firearms quotes. Other participants doubted the set because none of the quotes is on Lenin’s Wikiquote page.

items.who: “A system of licensing and registration is the perfect device to deny gun ownership to the bourgeoisie”
items.why: A Skeptics Stack Exchange question ↗ found this companion quote all over the internet but with no speech, publication or year. The top answer quotes They Never Said It, which calls it “highly improbable” that Lenin, who died in 1924, said anything useful to opponents of US firearms registration in the late twentieth century.

misattribution.truthLine: Nothing Lenin wrote or said is known to contain this line. The nearest genuine text is his December 1917 note “The man with the gun need no longer be feared” ↗, which makes a different point.

context.heading: Why the real phrase points the other way
lead: Lenin did write about “the man with the gun”. While on a short vacation in Finland in late December 1917, he jotted down themes for articles. The first was “The man with the gun need no longer be feared” ↗. According to the editors’ note, he had heard the remark in a railway carriage in Finland. The note was first published in 1929 in Lenin Miscellany XI, and it appears in English in Volume 36 of the Collected Works.

The popular line says something quite different: that whoever holds the gun rules the unarmed. That wording has never been traced to Lenin. Wikiquote dates its first appearance to the internet of the mid-1990s and does not name who wrote it.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator has no entry for this line. A search of its site turns up Lenin entries only for other quotes, such as the “rope” and printing-press lines.
Wikiquote’s Lenin page and its talk page both treat the line as unsourced. Nobody in those discussions or in the forum threads offers a speech, article, letter or date.
context.pull: The man with the gun need no longer be feared.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Lenin page lists 'One man with a gun can control 100 without one.' in its Misattributed section with the note 'Not found in Lenin's Collected Works. Began to surface on the internet in the mid-1990s.'
Wikiquote talk page has a thread on the line: 'I've seen this quote pop up a lot, but have never seen a credible source to back it up. Did Lenin really say this?'

Lenin's 'From a Publicist's Diary' (written Dec 24-27, 1917 in Finland; first published 1929 in Lenin Miscellany XI; CW vol. 36, pp. 460-463) lists theme 1 'The man with the gun need no longer be feared.' The editors' note says he heard the remark in a car on the Finnish railway.
Marxists.org hosts an index of Lenin's Collected Works.
In a Straight Dope thread the line is posted unsourced among Lenin gun quotes, and a participant notes none appear on Lenin's Wikiquote page.

Skeptics SE question on the Lenin 'licensing and registration' quote finds no source; the top answer quotes They Never Said It calling it 'highly improbable' that Lenin, who died in 1924, said anything useful to late-20th-century US opponents of firearms registration.
